headline: Two Long-Legged Cats Unlock Mystery of Rare Human Genetic Disorder
meta_description: Cornell researchers identify first confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats, opening new doors for veterinary diagnostics and genetic testing.
summary_short: Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy helped scientists make a rare discovery: the first documented cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats.
body:
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy have helped Cornell University researchers achieve a genetic breakthrough that extends far beyond the feline world. Scientists at the College of Veterinary Medicine identified the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats—a rare connective tissue disorder that affects approximately 1 in 4,000 people. The brothers' unusually long limbs first caught veterinarians' attention when they were kittens, but as they grew older, additional abnormalities emerged: structural problems in their eyes and an enlarged aorta. These combined symptoms pointed to a condition previously thought to occur only in humans. Their case, published in Scientific Reports, provides the first genetically confirmed evidence of this disease in cats.

The breakthrough came through detailed medical examinations and DNA analysis. Researchers discovered that Gary and Shaggy each carried two altered copies of the FBN1 gene, which provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1—a protein essential for healthy connective tissue supporting blood vessels, bones, ligaments, skin, and eyes. Inheriting one mutated copy from each parent was exceptionally unusual; in humans, just one altered copy is often enough to cause Marfan syndrome. Yet the brothers' particular genetic variant had an unexpected silver lining: it didn't completely disable the gene but instead interfered with how its instructions were processed while allowing some normal activity to continue.

This partial function explains why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying such a severe genetic load. According to senior author Dr. Jacquelyn Evans, assistant professor at the Baker Institute for Animal Health, "The findings provide a foundation for improved veterinary diagnostics. It can help veterinarians recognize similar cases in the future and may help develop genetic tests." Their remarkable story offers veterinarians new tools for diagnosis and a clearer understanding of how genetic mutations can produce variable outcomes—knowledge that benefits both cats and humans.
quick_facts: Cornell researchers identified first genetic cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy showed unusually long limbs and eye abnormalities
Both cats inherited two altered copies of the FBN1 gene, exceptionally rare in animals
Marfan syndrome affects approximately 1 in 4,000 humans
Findings published in Scientific Reports, October 2026
